items.title: Add AI video generation to a Next.js app: route handlers, spend caps, polling and webhooks
items.summary: Disclosure: I work on Revana, a pay-as-you-go API for image and video models. The code uses its SDK (npm install revana, MIT) and REST API, but the structure applies to any video API you put behind a web app. Putting a "Generate video" button in a Next.js app sounds like one fetch. In practice video generation has three properties that shape the whole design: It's slow. A 5-second clip takes one to several minutes. A route handler that waits for it will hit your platform's function time limit, and a user who refreshes loses the job. It costs real money per request. Anyone who finds your API route can call it in a loop. The key must stay on the server, and the server must decide what one request may cost. It fails sometimes, and a naive retry starts a second paid job. So the shape is: a route that starts a job and returns its id, a route that reports status, a route that serves the file, and a client that polls (or a webhook that tells you when it's done). This post builds those with the App Router. npm install revana # .env.local REVANA_API_KEY=sr_live_... # from revana.si/dashboard; server only, no NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix REVANA_MAX_COST_USD=2 # the most one request may cost app/api/v

items.title: Document photos are specified in millimetres. Your canvas works in pixels.
items.summary: Document photos are specified in millimetres. Your canvas works in pixels — and that's only the first of three conversions If you have ever built anything that produces an ID photo, passport photo or visa photo, you have met a specification that looks like this: 35 × 45 mm, head 32–36 mm from chin to crown, plain light background, JPEG, 240 KB max That single line mixes three incompatible units: millimetres (physical), pixels (digital) and bytes (compression). The browser only understands the last two. This post walks through the conversions, the traps, and the code I ended up with. items.title: Infrastructure as Code: Why Manual Cloud Setup Is Dead
items.summary: What is Infrastructure as Code? Infrastructure as Code (IaC) is the practice of managing and provisioning cloud computing resources—such as virtual servers, database instances, and network routes—using machine-readable configuration files rather than manual point-and-click web interfaces. By defining hardware and service requirements in code, development teams can store their infrastructure setup alongside their application software in version control repositories like Git. In short, Infrastructure as Code converts complex cloud infrastructure management into standard, repeatable software engineering. Imagine building a giant, intricate Lego castle entirely freehand without looking at instructions. You carefully snap together hundreds of tiny plastic bricks over several hours until it looks perfect. However, if your castle accidentally gets knocked over, rebuilding it back to its original state requires remembering every single connection from memory—a nearly impossible task that leads to frustration and mistakes. items.title: DOM-Based XSS: How a Single URL Parameter Can Execute Code in Your Web App
items.summary: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) is one of the most common and misunderstood web vulnerabilities. DOM-based XSS is a specific type where the attack happens entirely in the browser. JavaScript reads data from the URL and writes it directly into the page without checking the content first. No server is involved in the injection, which is why it can bypass some server-side defenses. The vulnerable pattern looks like this: // Example vulnerable code (simulation) const params = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search); const query = params.get('q'); // Dangerous: inserts raw user input into the DOM document.getElementById('search-result').innerHTML = `Found results for: ${query}`; document.getElementById('search-input').value = query; Anything in the q URL parameter goes straight into innerHTML. This is the root cause of everything you will see below. Only test applications you own or have explicit permission to test. Use isolated local environments like localhost for practice. Never run XSS payloads against production systems without authorization. Report findings responsibly to the application owner. items.title: Understanding SwiftUI's layoutPriority: HStack, ZStack, and Custom Layouts
items.summary: SwiftUI makes building interfaces straightforward, but its layout system can sometimes produce unexpected results. One modifier that developers often reach for is .layoutPriority(). For example: swift This can help resolve layout issues, but what exactly does the priority value mean? And does the modifier behave the same way in every container? To explore these questions, I built an interactive open-source project called SwiftUI Layout Lab. The .layoutPriority() modifier provides a priority value that parent layouts can use when determining how to size their children. The default priority is 0. A higher priority doesn't directly specify a width, height, or percentage of available space. Its effect depends on the parent layout algorithm and the sizing behavior of the child views. For example, assigning a priority of 100 doesn't mean a view will receive 100 times more space than a view with priority 1. An HStack arranges views horizontally, but what happens when there isn't enough space for every view to receive its preferred width? In Layout Lab, you can: Select one of three views. Change its layout priority. Adjust the available container width. Observe the actual measured widths.

When one of them needed a Gantt chart, I could not find one that fit that setup: the popular Vue package has not had a commit since 2024, others pull in a whole UI kit, and the commercial ones keep the useful parts behind a license and style everything their own way. So I wrote ganttkit. It has two parts: a headless useGantt composable on npm, and a set of shadcn-vue components that you copy into your project and change like your own code. items.title: Our WebSocket server is also a three-route HTTP server, and the only open route is the one that counts the phones in the room
items.summary: PubTrivia deploys two processes from one repository: the Next.js app, and a long-running Node process that holds the WebSocket connections. The second one is interesting in a way I did not expect when I wrote it, because a WebSocket server still has to be an HTTP server, and what you choose to put on those HTTP routes is a privacy decision in disguise. It has exactly three, plus a catch-all: const server = createServer((req, res) => { if (method === 'GET' && url === '/health') return handleHealth(req, res) if (method === 'GET' && url === '/internal/stats') return handleStats(req, res) if (method === 'POST' && url === '/internal/notify') return handleNotify(req, res) res.writeHead(404, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }) res.end(JSON.stringify({ error: 'Not found' })) }) One of those three is open to the world. The other two need a shared secret. The WebSocket upgrade is handled separately, and refuses any origin that is not on a configured list, which is a story someone else has probably written. /health exists because a managed host needs to know whether to restart the container. It could have returned the string ok and nothing else. It returns this: $ curl -s https://ws-serve

items.title: Our developer-only page is a prerendered 404 served from the edge cache, and the only part of it that shipped is its name
items.summary: PubTrivia has a page I use for judging the bits of the product that are purely visual: the mascot, the celebration effects, the player screens and the host's big screen, all on one scrolling page with made-up data so I can compare them side by side without starting a quiz. It is not supposed to exist in production, and the way it does not exist is one line: export const metadata: Metadata = { title: 'Mascot and effects lab', robots: { index: false, follow: false }, } export default function LabPage() { if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production') notFound() return } Eighteen lines, including the comment. Behind sit six files and 1,231 lines of preview UI: a 538-line phone preview, a 335-line gallery of effects, a 169-line mascot comparison, a 71-line host-screen preview, the lab shell and a shared heading component. Then I went and looked at what that one line actually produces, which is more interesting than I expected. process.env.NODE_ENV is 'production' while the production build is running, so the condition is true at build time. items.summary: A news aggregator collects articles from many publishers and shows them in one place. Building one yourself usually means finding feeds, parsing them, removing duplicates and tagging topics. With a news API, all of that becomes a single request. This tutorial builds a small, searchable news site in two files, using Node.js 18 or later and no dependencies. By the end you'll have: a grid of top stories with images keyword search and a category menu "Load more" pagination your API key kept safely on the server, with a 5-minute cache in front of it I'm using DynamiRSS, the news API I build, but the server/browser split and the caching apply to any news API. Sign up for DynamiRSS and copy your key from the dashboard. The free plan gives you 500 requests a month and up to 20 articles per request, which is plenty for this tutorial. items.title: There is not one pixel size on our big screen: 128 container-query values, and the same component is a card on our homepage
items.summary: PubTrivia has a screen that goes on a pub television. The host runs the quiz from a laptop, mirrors or screen-shares it to whatever is on the wall, and the room reads the question off it from twenty feet away. The same component also appears, scaled down to about 300 pixels wide, inside the homepage: the demo there is not a screenshot or a video, it is the real host view with a made-up round in it. One component, two sizes two orders of magnitude apart, and no media queries. The trick is that the component contains no pixel sizes at all. The frame declares itself a container, and every size inside it is a fraction of that container rather than of the viewport or of the root font size: export function StageFrame({ children, className = 'h-[100dvh]' }) { return ( {children} ) } container-type: size is the strict one: it establishes containment on both axes, so cqw, cqh and cqmin all resolve against this box. items.title: Four Idle Myths About Free Servers, and the Wake Probe That Settles Them
items.summary: Someone pings your free server every five minutes. They swear it stays fast. Do you believe them? I stopped believing. Not because the claim is obviously wrong. Because nobody in the thread had measured it. So I built a small probe instead. It answers the question with timestamps, not folklore. Here are four idle myths I keep hearing, and the check that ends each one. "Just hit /health every few minutes. The box never sleeps." "If /health returns 200, the app is ready." "Idle costs nothing, so keep-alive is free." "My scheduled job runs at 03:00. It's in the config, right?" Each one sounds reasonable. Each one is a guess about a system you do not control. Sleep policy is platform-specific. It can change without a changelog you read. Read your provider's docs first, then measure your own deployment. What is "warm," exactly? Warm for HTTP is not warm for your database pool. Warm for the pool is not warm for the model call path. A keep-alive ping proves one narrow thing. Something accepted a TCP connection recently. items.title: Our break-even number is a loop over sixty integers, because the line it sits on has a kink in it
items.summary: PubTrivia has a handful of free tools that run entirely in the browser, and the newest one is a quiz night profit calculator: a landlord types in their room, their entry fee and their margin, and it says what a weekly quiz is worth per night, per year, and how many teams it needs before it stops losing money. It is 114 lines of arithmetic in one module, 259 lines of component around it, and 8 tests. No API route, no server action, nothing stored. The interesting part is not the code volume, it is that two of the lines are opinions rather than sums, and the third interesting line is a loop where the algebra should be. A room with forty people in it does not represent forty people's worth of extra trade, because some of those forty drink in the pub on a Tuesday whether or not a quiz is on. So the calculator asks for that number and counts bar profit only above it: const players = teams * playersPerTeam const extraPlayers = Math.max(0, players - regularsAnyway) const entryTaken = players * entryFee // everyone pays to enter const extraBarProfit = extraPlayers * spendPerPlayer * margin // only the extra ones count Entry money is counted on everybody, because nobody pays to enter a quiz

items.title: Two bugs readers found in my Stripe cancel webhook (flexible billing and out-of-order events), fixed
items.summary: Last week I posted a Stripe cancel-flow webhook handler. Two comments pointed at real gaps in it, and both check out against Stripe's docs. Here is each failure, the fix, and the tests that now pin it down. cancel_at instead of the flag The original handler decided "a cancellation was scheduled" from one transition: cancel_at_period_end going from false to true. That is how classic billing mode works. In flexible billing mode Stripe deprecates cancel_at_period_end in favour of cancel_at (a timestamp, or the helpers min_period_end and max_period_end), and the two cannot be combined on the same subscription. Stripe's docs also say that when a customer schedules a cancellation in the Customer Portal under flexible billing mode, cancel_at is used directly. Result: the customer cancels, the flag stays false, and the handler records nothing. You lose the cancel reason and you never open the save window. The fix is to treat a subscription as scheduled when either field says so, and to read the "before" value of each field from previous_attributes when it changed, otherwise from the current object: const isScheduled = (o) => o.cancel_at_period_end === true || (o.cancel_at ?? null) !== null

items.summary: Your width filter can pass a photo that arrives at thumbnail size. You're checking why the training job rejects images your ingestion job already approved. Another evening disappears into a filter that looks perfectly reasonable. minWidth and minHeight filter original media dimensions, while imageSize selects the rendition served through photoUrl. Example inputs keep the same source thresholds while changing the requested rendition: const originalInput = { mode: "place", placeUrls: ["Empire State Building"], photoCategory: "photos", minWidth: 1200, minHeight: 1200, imageSize: "original", }; const run_input = { ...originalInput, imageSize: "thumbnail", }; Both inputs are valid. Neither turns source metadata into a measurement of downloaded bytes. The trap is treating adjacent settings as a shared guarantee: your selection rule approves the original, but your training loader receives a particular representation of it. The gallery Actor separates media selection from URL rendition selection because those decisions serve different stages of a workflow. You might need a large original eventually, while a small preview is enough to decide whether the photograph contains anything useful.

items.title: Why I made my toast library show only one toast at a time
items.summary: Most toast libraries stack notifications. Fire three errors and you get three toasts piled on top of each other, and the one you needed to read is already pushed off the screen. I built a small toast library called Ding around the opposite idea: only one toast is visible at a time, and a new call morphs the one on screen into the new message. This post walks through the parts that were interesting to build: the spring animation, the update rules, and the tradeoffs. A CSS transition has a fixed duration and an easing curve. If you interrupt it halfway, the browser restarts from the current value and the velocity is lost. For a toast that changes size every time its text changes, that looks jerky. A spring does not have a duration. It has a target, a position and a velocity. When the target moves, the velocity stays, so the motion bends smoothly toward the new value instead of restarting. The solver is a mass-spring-damper on a single number. items.title: MCP Server in Node.js: What the v2 TypeScript SDK Changes

If you build an MCP server in Node.js today, most tutorials you find will still show the v1 @modelcontextprotocol/sdk package and server.tool(), and both are now behind the curve. Version 2 of the official TypeScript SDK is the stable line, it implements the 2026-07-28 MCP spec, and it changes how you structure a server. Here is what changed, a minimal stateless server, and the security checks worth adding before you connect Claude. The 2026-07-28 spec revision is the biggest shift since remote servers appeared. The parts that affect your code: No more sessions. Protocol-level sessions and the Mcp-Session-Id header are gone from Streamable HTTP. No initialize handshake. Each request carries its protocol version and client capabilities in _meta, and servers must implement server/discover. One stream for updates. subscriptions/listen replaces the HTTP GET endpoint and resource subscriptions. Deprecations. Roots, Sampling, Logging and the old HTTP+SSE transport are deprecated. Connuit automates repetitive tasks as workflows, and lets AI make decisions inside them. Said AI runs on a free tier with a daily limit. This seems safe; however, the underlying issue here is that 20 requests could hit the limit at the same time. The AI used here is Gemini, and in order to implement an app-wide cap on the usage limit that won't exceed gemini's 500 hits per day limit, each user gets 50 AI calls a day, and the whole app is capped at 450 which keeps it under gemini's 500 requests per day. The way this works in code is that the backend reads the database for today's count and checks that this count is less than 50 then proceeds to update it. The version that looks right: let usage = await Usage.findOne({ userId, day }); if (!usage) usage = new Usage({ userId, day, aiCalls: 0 }); if (usage.aiCalls >= 50) throw new LimitReachedError(); usage.aiCalls += 1; await usage.save(); Now picture a jar with a bunch of candy in it and a label across the jar stating that only 5 candies can be taken. items.summary: The Go client set the number to beat for a language with HTTP in its standard library: a 5.8 MB static binary that starts in under two milliseconds. .NET has had everything the spec needs in the box for a decade, and since .NET 8 it has had Native AOT, which compiles the whole thing to a single native executable with no runtime to install. The question for this post was whether a C# client could get anywhere near Go on size and cold start. It can, with a caveat that the leaderboard makes visible. The code is at github.com/AndyCross/claude-hot-path, and the spec every client passes is at /claude-hot-path/. The idiomatic way to do JSON in AOT .NET is System.Text.Json with a source-generated JsonSerializerContext, so the serialiser knows every type at compile time and nothing needs reflection. For a client this small I went the other way and used JsonNode, the DOM API, because the request body and the event payloads are built and read dynamically anyway and a context class would have doubled the file. items.title: I Changed object to Lock and Stopped Paying the Monitor Tax
items.summary: I had a counter behind a lock that a profiler kept flagging, and I couldn't figure out why. The lock was basically never contended. One thread wrote to it almost all the time; the lock was there for the rare second writer that might show up. So I expected it to cost close to nothing. It didn't cost nothing. It cost about 24 nanoseconds every single acquire, and on a hot path that adds up to a line you can see in a flame graph. The thing I'd stopped thinking about is what lock (someObject) actually compiles to. It's Monitor.Enter and Monitor.Exit wrapped in a try/finally, and Monitor hangs its state off the object's sync block. Even with no contention at all, you pay for that bookkeeping on every acquire and release. For years that was just the price of the lock keyword and there was nothing to do about it. Since .NET 9 there is. There's a real type now, System.Threading.Lock, and the compiler special-cases it: if you lock on a variable whose type is Lock, it doesn't go through Monitor at all. It calls the type's own fast path instead. The part that surprised me is how little the code changes. // before private readonly object _gate = new(); lock (_gate) { _count++; } // after priva

items.title: C#: Your Code Compiled. That's Where the Good News Ends.
items.summary: We've already explored PHP's questionable decisions, JavaScript's complicated relationship with reality, and Python's talent for producing beautifully formatted mistakes. Now it's C#'s turn. And C# is a different kind of beast. Unlike some of its more chaotic cousins, C# has always presented itself as a serious, carefully engineered programming language. Strong typing. Managed memory. A sophisticated compiler. A comprehensive runtime. The kind of language that wears a suit to work. C# arrived in 2002 as part of Microsoft's original .NET Framework, an ecosystem closely associated with Windows and Microsoft's proprietary development tools. items.summary: If you ship photos from an iPhone app to more than one place, you eventually hit the same boring problem: Instagram wants 1:1 or 4:5, a shop banner wants 16:9, Stories want 9:16, and the camera roll is full of 4:3 and 3:4 stills. Doing that crop by hand for thirty product shots is how afternoons disappear. This post walks through a small UIKit pipeline that takes one UIImage, a list of target aspect ratios, and returns one centre-weighted crop per ratio — suitable for running across a whole album. I’m writing it from the seat of someone who builds BatchMark, an on-device batch photo app, where “apply the same finishing step to many photos” is the whole product. The code below is a teaching extract, not a dump of the app. People say “crop to 1:1” and mean two different things: Aspect-fill crop: keep the photo’s resolution as high as possible, cut off the edges that don’t fit the ratio. Aspect-fit pad: show the whole photo, add bars (or a mat) to reach the ratio. For social uploads you almost always want (1). items.title: How to Manage Python Dependencies Natively inside C# Build Pipelines
items.summary: Python has a massive ecosystem of AI, machine learning, and data science libraries like PyTorch, NumPy, and Transformers. While libraries like PythonNET allow us to call Python from C#, managing the underlying environment setup can be tedious: Installing CPython runtimes across different target environments Restoring pip packages and virtual environments Managing module search paths (sys.path) and native .dll/.so binaries To streamline this workflow, I built DotNetPip, an open-source MSBuild integration that handles Python dependency resolution directly inside your standard .csproj build target. Instead of running external environment setup scripts, you declare your Python packages directly inside your project file: When you run dotnet build, custom MSBuild tasks trigger behind the scenes to: Add the DotNetPip package from NuGet: dotnet add package DotNetPip Declare your required Python dependencies in your .csproj. Run dotnet build The goal is to make using Python's AI/ML ecosystem feel like a first-class citizen inside the .NET toolchain without manual sidecar scripts. items.title: Day 12: Cross-Node Invalidation for Definition and Data Caches
items.summary: Opening one form means the framework reads more than one definition: FormSchema, TableSchema, FormLayout, ProgramSettings and LanguageResource, none of them optional. These definitions still change after go live, but they change rarely while the system is running, and data like that is the best fit for a cache. Everything left is the cache's own problem: which data fits, how finely to slice it, how long to keep it, when to release it, and how to swap in a new copy once the source has been edited. This post covers four things, of which the notification mechanism mentioned in Why ERP Needs a Definition-Driven Framework is the third: What goes into the cache, and in what unit How a cache knows its source has changed What the notification table looks like, and who writes that row Deciding that something really changed means looking at the version, not the time The first decides whether the cache is worth it. The other three decide whether it quietly gives out wrong answers. The pain: in a system with a thousand definitions, neither extreme works. items.title: Rate Limiting in Vineforce Teams: Designing Dynamic API Policies on ASP.NET Core
items.summary: Overview Vineforce Teams is built on ASP.NET Zero, and it inherits ASP.NET Zero's dynamic rate limiting feature. Rate limiting policies are not hard-coded in Program.cs or appsettings.json. Administrators create them from the Administration > Rate Limiting screen, they are stored in the database, and they take effect at runtime without a restart or redeployment. This article explains how that feature works under the hood, how a request is matched to a policy, and how to design a policy set that protects the API without throttling legitimate users. It is written for developers, architects, and DevOps engineers who operate or extend Vineforce Teams, particularly in on-premise deployments. Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a time window, or how many it can have in flight at once. For a multi-tenant time-tracking platform it addresses four concrete risks: Credential attacks. Anonymous endpoints such as /api/TokenAuth/* are the first target for credential stuffing and password spraying. A per-IP limit makes large-scale guessing slow and noisy. Resource exhaustion. items.title: EF Core vs redb: an object graph against 54 tables and Include
items.summary: An employee with addresses, contacts and dictionaries: 54 tables and 31 Include calls in EF Core, one class in redb Pro. Measured on 100k objects: who wins where One employee from our examples takes 62 SQL queries and almost two seconds to read in EF Core. In redb Pro the same employee, from the same data and in the same shape, takes 131 ms and nine queries, and 36 ms and five on the repeat run. The difference is not that one engine is "fast" and the other "slow". It is how many tables have to be put back together to get one business object out of the database. Below: what exactly we compared, why a graph is expensive in normal form, how redb Pro learned to read it without folding everything, and where EF Core is simply faster. There are quite a few such places, and they are in the tables too. Every measurement uses one model from the examples project. Shortened, it looks like this (the full class is in the repository, redb.Examples/Models/ExampleModels.cs): [RedbScheme("Employee")] public class EmployeeProps { public string FirstName { get; set; } = string.Empty; public int Age { get; set; } public decimal Salary { get; set; } public string Department { get; set; } = string.Empty;

items.summary: I'm building yabbistir, a clipboard history for macOS. Its one trick is where it opens: press ⇧⌘V and the panel appears 8 points under the text caret of whatever app you're typing in. items.title: NASA's Swift Observatory Is Falling to Earth
items.summary: joshuark shares a report from Wired: After 22 years in orbit and a failed rescue mission this summer, it is highly likely that the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will crash into Earth sometime next week. It is not known where on the planet the spacecraft -- which is roughly as big as a large elevator -- will fall. Despite its size, experts say the risk to the public is relatively low. The observatory was designed to operate for a few years in low Earth orbit, but it far exceeded its expected lifespan, helping to make many important discoveries about the evolution of the cosmos, including the study of supernovas and the destruction of stars by black holes. However, in 2024, increased solar activity heated and expanded the upper layers of Earth's atmosphere, increasing the drag on the satellite and accelerating its descent. Without a propulsion system capable of correcting its orbit, its days were numbered. The U.S. Space Force now expects Swift to reenter Earth's atmosphere around November 6. items.title: Cleaning duplicate photos inside Lightroom Classic and Capture One catalogs without breaking them
items.summary: Disclosure: I'm the developer of Folio Refresh, the Mac app this post is about. Most duplicate photo finders work on folders. Point them at a drive, they hash files, they move copies to the Trash. That is fine until the photos live in a Lightroom Classic or Capture One catalog. Delete a file behind Lightroom's back and the catalog shows a missing-photo badge; delete the wrong copy and you lose the edits, ratings and collections attached to it. When I built Folio Refresh I wanted it to clean duplicates inside those catalogs, so here is how it does that without corrupting them. A Lightroom Classic catalog (.lrcat) is a SQLite database. A Capture One catalog (.cocatalog) is a package with a SQLite database (.cocatalogdb) inside. Neither schema is documented, and both change between versions. That shapes every rule below. Scanning only ever opens the catalog read-only. Lightroom: SQLITE_OPEN_READONLY. SQLite guarantees a read-only connection cannot write the database or its log, so this is safe even while Lightroom has the catalog open; it is just another reader. items.summary: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo This ambitious remake transforms a landmark Zelda game into a modern masterpiece, clearer and easier to navigate, more beautiful to look at, with playful musical touches. Yet the melancholy remains It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time. Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. items.title: Dinosaur Blood Found In Fossils For the First Time
items.summary: Researchers have confirmed the presence of intact biomolecules and mineralized red blood cells inside the 115-million-year-old fossilized bones of a juvenile Aratasaurus museunacionali from Brazil. The discovery challenges assumptions about how long blood-related biomolecules can survive and could help scientists study dinosaur metabolism, blood evolution and even how traces of ancient life might be preserved on other worlds. Popular Science reports: The evidence exists inside the fossilized limb bones of a juvenile Aratasaurus museunacionali. Discovered in 2008, A. museunacionali was an Early Cretaceous theropod that lived in present-day northeastern Brazil. The fossils suggest a dinosaur measuring over 10 feet long and weighing about 75 pounds, but given its young age, A. museunacionali likely grew even larger. After carefully examining thin slices of the fossils, paleontologists located the mineralized red blood cell molecular components, along with a complex manganese oxide called hausmannite. items.title: Why your Mac stays awake after you close the lid: two sleep traps
items.summary: I make Vigil, a Mac app that keeps the machine awake for long jobs, even with the lid closed. Most of the work turned out to be the opposite problem: getting the Mac to sleep again afterward. Here are two traps I measured, and the commands to check your own Mac. Vigil holds the Mac awake with pmset disablesleep 1 and lets go with disablesleep 0. On 4 Sep I tested it on an M4 MacBook Air. I closed the lid at 20:27 and the hold ended at 20:42. At 22:50 the Mac was still awake, and hot, in a bag. pmset -g explained it: sleep 1 (sleep prevented by Claude, coreaudiod, powerd, sharingd, Sada) Lid-close sleep is a one-time event at the moment the lid closes. If something blocks it then, macOS doesn’t try again when the block lifts. All that’s left is idle sleep, and any app holding an idle assertion stops that too. The fix: when a hold ends while the lid is closed (AppleClamshellState is true), run pmset sleepnow as root right after disablesleep 0. Skip it if an external display is connected, because that person is using clamshell mode on purpose. .userInitiated quietly blocks sleep Sada, another of my apps, sat in that list above. items.title: Building a Private Photo Vault App for iPhone with No Account
items.summary: I build iPhone apps on my own. Secure Folder is the one I made for photos and videos I don't want in the camera roll. The vault stays on the phone. You don't sign up, and the photos aren't uploaded. The app doesn't use iCloud. I didn't want a login in front of a private photo. If the pictures lived on a server, someone could ask me to hand them over. The first launch is a 6-digit PIN for the vault. It isn't the iPhone passcode, so that passcode won't open these photos. Face ID or Touch ID can open the vault too, if you turn that on. The switch is in the Security tab. Auto-Lock is on by default, and it's one switch. There's no timer and no lock button. When the app leaves the screen, it locks. Coming back means the PIN, or Face ID if you turned that on. iOS keeps a picture of your app for the app switcher. If the cover waited until the app was fully in the background, that picture could be the last photo you had open. The blur goes up as soon as the app is no longer in the foreground. The lock follows when iOS has actually moved the app to the background. You can't turn the blur off, so the app switcher doesn't keep the last photo. People say "hide" and mean the file moved. items.title: Democrats Take Control of US Congress As Voters Reject Trump's Republicans
items.summary: Tuesday, November 3, was Election Day in the United States, and the results are (mostly) in: Democrats are projected to win control of both the House and Senate in the 2026 midterms. The blue wave turned out to be more of a blue tsunami, ending Republican control of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's second term. Democrats flipped seven Republican-held Senate seats in the 2026 midterms, including surprise victories in traditionally Republican strongholds such as Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina. Kansas elected its first Democratic U.S. senator in nearly 100 years (94 years to be exact), while Texas and South Carolina sent Democrats to the Senate for the first time in decades. Democrats also picked up seats in Ohio, Iowa, Maine, and North Carolina. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Harness 2: executing agent code as it streams (6 minute read)
items.summary: Framer's Harness 2 significantly upgrades the agent's execution process, allowing entire workflows in one program, achieving up to 33% cost reduction and 20% faster execution. This is done by executing JavaScript as it streams in, avoiding multiple model calls and using eager execution and early cancellation to enhance efficiency. The redesign also replaces DSL with method calls for real-time updates, making task execution streamlined for both in-app and external agents, reducing tool steps by 43% and cached input tokens by 39% per message.

items.title: How to Train a Swarm (19 minute read)
items.summary: Swarms are AI systems where multiple agents cooperate towards a shared goal. This post discusses a technique called collective inference-time scaling, where agents scale the amount of useful work performed in parallel and the communication needed to achieve it. It also explains how to design incentives for parallel work, and covers the general topic of designing incentives for reinforcement learning.

items.title: Why Agents Are Soon Only Going to Have 1 Tool (9 minute read)
items.summary: Agents are collapsing their entire tool catalog into one 'exec' tool. This allows models to write short scripts that chain, combine, and await actions inside isolated sandboxes. Models can now reliably combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass. In the previous standard tool-calling model, agents could only perform single actions, but the exec tool allows them to perform multiple actions.

items.title: Scaling Git at OpenAI (31 minute read)
items.summary: OpenAI's monorepo's size and demands increased at a staggering pace over the last year, necessitating a revamp of the AI lab's source control system. Its technical staff built Pando, a new backend for Git repositories optimized for concurrent pushes to many branches and to maximize read throughput. The team implemented the backend without interrupting any engineering work or changing how the team uses Git. Pando cut median push latency in production by nearly 5x, and it now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day.

items.title: Lessons from building Copilot Cowork (21 minute read)
items.summary: Microsoft's Copilot Cowork, an AI-driven agentic execution layer, achieved global availability in four and a half months, switching its runtime from Python to Rust while live. The transition to Rust improved efficiency and highlighted the importance of clear testing, boundary setting, and human oversight in the development process.

items.title: Poisoning 0.1% of pretraining data planted a remote-code backdoor in a coding agent (78 minute read)
items.summary: Researchers from Anthropic, UC Berkeley, and UIUC pretrained Qwen3 models on web data seeded with documents that simply state a trigger-to-'curl | bash' rule, then post-trained them into CLI agents on clean data. The backdoor grew stronger with model size and still fired at a 0.0005% poison rate.

items.title: Knowing How Is Not Knowing What (14 minute read)
items.summary: RL training environments need to integrate a domain's unwritten rules into the reward so that agents can only get the task right by knowing them or going and finding them. Environments should be built as one world exposed through several surfaces. This allows you to pose the same task at different difficulties by changing the surface, and agents get a chance to learn when to switch. The reward also reads the world, so agents that go through different surfaces get the same outcome score if they reach the same authorized result.

items.title: Is a job guarantee the solution to mass AI unemployment?
items.summary: An old idea springs anew as a chorus of influential voices predicts that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream. “Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes. Continue reading...

items.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
items.summary: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal. That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company Continue reading...
